content: The Evelyn tables are a collection of four anatomical specimens mounted on wooden boards, believed to be the oldest anatomical preparations in Europe. These specimens were acquired by John Evelyn in 1646 during his visit to Padua, Italy, and were later donated to the Royal Society. Currently, the tables are owned by the Royal College of Surgeons and are displayed at the Hunterian Museum in London. Additionally, six similar anatomical tables are held by the Royal College of Physicians, which were brought to London from Italy by John Finch. Each of the Evelyn tables represents a specific part of the human anatomy. The dissections were meticulously prepared from human specimens and adhered to wooden boards made of pine planks, which were planed, glued together, and coated with multiple layers of varnish for preservation. The dimensions of each table are approximately 1.9 meters in height, 77 centimeters in width, and 10 centimeters in thickness. The first table illustrates the spinal cord and associated nerves. The second table depicts the aorta and the arterial system. The third table showcases the vagus nerves, sympathetic nerves, and the veins of the lungs and liver. The fourth table demonstrates the distribution of the venous system. John Evelyn, an English writer and diarist, spent several years abroad during the 1640s, a period coinciding with the English Civil War. His diary notes a visit to the University of Padua in March 1646, where he attended dissection lectures and acquired the four anatomical tables. A later letter from Evelyn mentions that he purchased the tables for 150 scudi. Three of the tables—those displaying the arteries, nerves, and veins—were prepared by Giovanni Leoni d'Este, who served as the dissector for Johann Vesling, the Professor of Anatomy at Padua. These three tables were originally created for Leoni's personal use. The fourth table, which features the vagus nerves, lungs, and liver, was specifically prepared by Leoni at Evelyn's request. After acquiring the tables, Evelyn continued his travels before eventually returning to London. His diary records the arrival of the tables in London in April 1649, following delays during their transport via Venice and Holland. In October 1667, Evelyn donated the tables to the newly established Royal Society. The tables were displayed in the Society's repository (museum) located in the west gallery of Gresham College on Bishopsgate starting in 1674. On January 21, 1701, William Cowper presented a paper on the tables of arteries and veins to the Royal Society. This paper was later published in the Philosophical Transactions, accompanied by illustrations engraved by Michael van der Gucht. After the Royal Society relocated to Crane Court, off Fleet Street, the tables were eventually acquired by the British Museum in June 1781. In 1809, the tables were purchased by the Royal College of Surgeons, where they remain to this day.
